newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks rise from Florida court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks rise from Florida court ruling.

text.p: The stocks of tobacco companies jumped Tuesday on news that a judge dismissed pre-1994 claims in a landmark lawsuit brought against the industry by the state of Florida to recover Medicaid payments.

"It's like these stocks have been through a very bad storm and now you're beginning to see the sky brighten a bit," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown & Catherwood, a money management firm that owns shares of tobacco giant Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
But Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles told reporters that the ruling Monday by a judge in West Palm Beach, Fla., had left the most important parts of the lawsuit intact.

"The court has pared down the suit," he said. "The good news for us is that we're left with our count of negligence and strict liability. We're also left with our count for injunctive relief to stop the targeting of our kids."

While tobacco company lawyers will likely seek similar rulings in other states, other tobacco litigation and potential Food and Drug Administration reform means the liability burden on tobacco companies is far from being lifted, industry analysts and legal experts said.

Meanwhile, Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan said Tuesday he has decided to sue tobacco companies to recover state taxpayers' portion of the billions of dollars the state has paid in smoking related health care costs.
Illinois would be the 16th state to file such a suit.
In the closely watched Florida suit, state officials hope to recoup more than $400 million a year in Medicaid payments for the care of tobacco-related illnesses since 1994.
Florida sued the industry under a controversial 1994 state law that stripped cigarette makers of most of their traditional defences in a liability lawsuit.
On the New York Stock Exchange, Philip Morris rose $2.125 to $94.125 after rising initially to $94.875.
RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., parent of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., gained 50 cents to $27. B.A.T Industries Plc, parent of Brown & Williamson, was up 75 cents at $14.50 on the American Stock Exchange.
Smokeless tobacco maker UST Inc. was up $1.25 to $30.875, and Loews Corp. was rose $1 to $79.75.
In his decision, West Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen threw out 15 of the state's 18 claims against the cigarette companies.
The judge ruled that a recent state Supreme Court decision held that those claims could not go forward under the 1994 Florida Medicaid Amendments.
The court held that "the state cannot proceed without identifying each individual recipient of Medicaid payments."
Chiles said the state had lost in Cohen's ruling what it had expected to lose.

Among other things, Cohen barred Florida from seeking reimbursement from the tobacco industry for Medicaid expenses incurred before 1994, when a law was passed allowing the state to seek such reimbursement.
The judge also ordered a second round of mediation to attempt to break the impasse without going to trial.

"We're willing to mediate. We have been to start with," Chiles said. "The court has determined we have three good counts of negligence and strict liability. It may be that they will know they are facing trial and they'll seek to mediate. We look forward to trying."
A July attempt to reach a settlement ended quickly without an agreement.
Subject to the state's ability to identify individual recipients, the state is permitted to go forward with its post-1994 claims for negligence, product liability, and injunctive relief.

In a statement, Philip Morris said the Florida case "provided the most significant test of the states' legal attempts to impose liability on the tobacco industry without introducing proof of individual smoking."
However, "I think the remaining claims give the states plenty of room to recover some money," said Melissa Ronan, a consultant with Litigation Analysis for Wall Street.
